title: Decision Boundary Design

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Decision boundary design specifies how consequential decisions are allocated in an AI-assisted product. The allocation distinguishes autonomous system action, human confirmation and independent human judgment.

The practice applies to decision points where the system makes a choice, executes an action or provides a recommendation that will shape later events. It is not limited to adding an override control. Decision boundary design identifies the decision boundary, calibrates the threshold for crossing it and implements the interaction that enforces it.

In products with no model, the equivalent design problem is the allocation between a touchscreen and a physical control, and between what an interface may assert and what the system beneath it can evidence. Those examples are not AI examples; their uncertainty concerns sources, links, protocols and clocks rather than model confidence.

## What decision boundary design does

Decision boundary design determines which decision points are appropriate for autonomous AI action, which require human confirmation and which require independent human judgment. The practice treats this allocation as a design and governance problem, not only as a technical configuration problem.

Autonomous AI action is appropriate when the consequence of error is low and reversible, AI confidence is high and the volume of decisions makes human review impractical. Human confirmation is appropriate when the consequence is moderate or the action is irreversible. Human independent judgment is appropriate when consequence is high, governance requires epistemic independence or AI data coverage is insufficient for the specific decision context.

The practice also determines how the interface records the difference between an AI recommendation and a human decision. A record that does not distinguish recommendation from decision weakens the boundary because it obscures who or what made the consequential choice.

## Boundary identification, calibration and implementation

Decision boundary design has three separate activities: boundary identification, boundary calibration and boundary implementation. Each activity answers a different question about the same decision point.

Boundary identification determines which decision points belong in each category. It asks whether the AI may act autonomously, whether a human must confirm the action, or whether the human must make an independent judgment with the AI as reference rather than recommendation.

Boundary calibration sets thresholds. It asks at what consequence level autonomous AI action becomes inappropriate, and at what AI confidence level recommendation becomes inappropriate without disclosure. These thresholds are design decisions informed by consequence analysis, governance requirements and operational context; they are not only technical parameters.

Boundary implementation designs the enforcing interaction. It specifies what happens at a consequential decision point, how confirmation is structured, how AI confidence is communicated at the moment of decision and how the interface distinguishes between the AI recommendation and the human decision in the record.

## Boundary calibration matters more than the presence of an override

Decision boundary design treats human override as an interaction design problem. A boundary can be technically present but not meaningful if it is cognitively expensive to cross, such as when the override is buried, dismissal requires multiple steps or the interface offers no support for the override decision.

The risk is default acceptance. Users may accept AI recommendations not because they agree with them, but because the path of least resistance leads to acceptance.

The interaction must make the boundary legible. Users should understand when they are acting on AI output and when they are acting on their own judgment. The friction must also be calibrated to the consequence of the decision rather than applied uniformly.

Uniform friction can train users to click through. Friction at consequential decision points protects the decisions that need protection without impeding decisions that do not need the same protection.

## When Creative Navy applies decision boundary design

Creative Navy applies decision boundary design after trust-and-oversight analysis and behavioural requirements definition have identified where boundaries are needed and why. At that point, decision boundary design specifies how the required boundaries are implemented in interaction behaviour.

Decision boundary design is also used during Concept Convergence when evaluating AI interaction patterns. Different design directions often contain implicit boundary positions, and making those positions explicit is necessary for comparing them.

In enterprise and regulated contexts, decision boundary design is used before governance review. The boundary map becomes part of the evidence that the product's human oversight structure is meaningful rather than nominal.

## Puraite AI systematic review boundary between AI assistance and independent human judgment

In the Puraite AI systematic review case, the decision boundary was methodologically defined. Inclusion and exclusion decisions had to be made by human reviewers exercising independent judgment. The AI's role was to assist rather than decide.

Blinded mode enforced the epistemic independence boundary. The AI recommendation was not shown before the human reviewer made an assessment. Without this implementation, the boundary would exist nominally because users could still override, but it would not be enforced because AI recommendations could anchor judgment before independence was possible.

Confidence display at decision points implemented calibration. When the AI recommendation was available, confidence was shown as a percentage alongside the recommendation. This applied in blinded mode after human assessment and in non-blinded sessions. Low-confidence AI recommendations required more active human attention than high-confidence recommendations.

Override parity implemented the principle that the boundary should not make the correct path harder than the compliant path. The override interaction was designed to require no more cognitive effort than acceptance.

## Callsign fraud detection boundary between model score, policy consequence and human configuration

In the Callsign fraud detection case, the decision boundary separated what the model decided, what policy decided and what the human decided. The model produced risk scores. The policy layer determined thresholds and workflow triggers. Human analysts configured policies and strategic exceptions.

Model and policy separation operated as an architectural boundary. Human analysts made decisions at the policy level, deciding which consequence applied to which risk score, rather than modifying model outputs. The interface did not allow model outputs to be changed; it allowed policy interpretation of those outputs to be configured.

Policy evaluation mode enforced a boundary between analysis and modification. The read-only mode allowed analysts to evaluate how a policy would behave against historical data, separated from the configuration mode where policies were modified. This prevented accidental live modifications during evaluation sessions.

Consequence threshold surfacing created visible friction at the point of modification. High-consequence policy changes affecting live transaction volumes above specified thresholds were flagged when modified, so the friction was calibrated to the impact of the change.

## Owkin K biomedical AI boundary between dataset scope and researcher action

In the Owkin K biomedical AI case, the decision boundary separated what K knows from what the researcher decides to act on. K's responses were bounded by dataset scope, and the boundary design made that scope visible.

Every response included the data sources it drew from. Responses approaching the edge of K's knowledge scope were flagged. The researcher's decision to act on K's output was therefore informed by visible information about the data basis for the response.

Query framing was also treated as a decision point. The entry experience was designed so that researchers framed their query with knowledge of K's capability scope before committing to a question. This moved the first meaningful decision earlier in the workflow: researchers decided whether to ask before they asked, rather than receiving an output and only then deciding whether to trust it.

## Hudex intelligence analysis boundary between AI summary and analyst exploration

In the Hudex intelligence analysis case, the boundary between AI-generated summary and expert analytical engagement was implemented through progressive disclosure.

The project overview acted as the boundary entry. It showed AI-generated high-level analysis, and the researcher decided whether to engage with detailed AI clustering based on the summary. The boundary between receiving an AI summary and engaging with AI analysis was explicit and controlled by the researcher rather than crossed automatically.

Within the dondogram, the depth of AI analysis visible was controlled by user action rather than displayed by default. This kept the boundary between AI output and analyst judgment legible because the analyst remained aware of when AI-generated structure was being received and when the analyst's own interpretation was being applied.

## Non-model examples show boundary design without AI inference

Four non-model engagements show the same practice allocating boundaries between what an interface may assert and what the system beneath it can evidence. These engagements are not AI work and should not be treated as AI-governance examples. Their uncertainty is a property of sources, links, protocols and clocks, not of model confidence.

In KISPE Space, the product boundary excluded autonomous operational decisions, inferred adversary classification or targeting, guaranteed service-quality prediction and substitution for existing command systems. The enforcing behavioural rule was that system errors never invent operational conclusions. A transport or access failure is reported as a transport or access failure, with what is still known from cache, and is not translated into a statement about adversaries, sensors or service status.

In Raymarine next-generation fixed-mount VHF work, send eligibility was a derived boundary. Whether a digital call could be transmitted was computed from recipient identity validity, record freshness, channel lawfulness under the active regional profile and station readiness. The computation was repeated at the moment of sending, so a recipient could not drift during preparation. A visible vessel was not necessarily a callable vessel when it lacked a usable registered identity.

In Schone Airspace Group uncrewed aircraft Mission Control, command eligibility was a derived boundary. Whether an action could be offered was computed from source freshness, link condition and channel permission, not from selection alone. Where link condition and sample freshness could not establish eligibility, availability was shown as unknown rather than ready. The accepted cost was reduced apparent immediacy in uncertain conditions in order to preserve the accuracy of command affordances.

In the European manufacturer engagement for uncrewed systems and tactical command-and-control software, the radial menu was made non-contextual because the system could not reliably determine whether a vehicle was airborne or on the ground. The design showed every option rather than asserting a distinction the system beneath it could not evidence. This was a boundary about system knowledge, not model confidence.

## Outputs of decision boundary design

Decision boundary design produces a boundary map. The boundary map identifies decision points, assigns each decision point to autonomous action, human confirmation or independent human judgment, and records the reason for that assignment.

Decision boundary design also produces interaction rules. These rules specify how the interface handles the decision point, how friction is introduced or avoided, how confidence or data scope is shown, and how the record separates AI recommendation from human decision.

In enterprise and regulated contexts, the boundary map can form part of governance evidence. Its purpose is to show that human oversight is meaningful in the interaction design, rather than only nominal in policy language.

## Boundaries and limits of the practice

Decision boundary design does not guarantee that a human will make the correct decision. It specifies where human judgment, confirmation or autonomous action belongs, and designs the interaction that enforces that allocation.

Decision boundary design also does not convert non-model systems into AI systems. In non-model examples, the relevant boundary is between what the interface may assert and what the underlying system can evidence. Those examples should not be read as claims about model inference, AI confidence or AI governance.

The available engagement evidence describes boundary structures and design decisions. It does not establish that any boundary prevented an error or incident.

## Related practices

Decision boundary design follows trust-and-oversight analysis for AI when that analysis has identified trust calibration failures and oversight gaps that require boundaries.

Decision boundary design also follows behavioural requirements definition because boundary requirements are one category of behavioural requirement. Behavioural requirements define what the product must make possible, prevent or distinguish; decision boundary design specifies the enforcing interaction at the decision point.
